finding.problem: The wording_only flag is a free parameter on propose_element, so whoever proposes an element decides whether an agent may confirm it. Nothing checks that the element really only fixes wording. An agent can propose with wording_only true and then confirm it through confirm_wording_element. This bypasses the human confirmation that confirm_element requires. The precondition only reads the self-declared flag.

findings.label: other-real
findings.why: The self-declared wording_only flag lets a proposer bypass human confirmation, which is a real weakness but not the seeded rule conflict itself.

finding.problem: Several rules still say only a person confirms an element, which the new action contradicts. The confirm_element description says 'Only a person confirms.' The glossary entry for element says 'confirmed only by a person.' The Element object description says 'proposed by an agent or confirmed by a person.' These were not updated.

findings.label: seeded
findings.why: It identifies that the new agent-confirm action contradicts the existing rule that only a person confirms an element, citing the unchanged descriptions.

finding.problem: An agent can now confirm an element in the 'unknown' state through the new matrix cell. The glossary says an unknown element 'stays visible until someone answers it'. Under the previous behaviour only a person could move an element out of unknown. Now an agent can silently resolve an unknown by setting wording_only.

findings.label: other-real
findings.why: The new matrix cell lets an agent resolve an unknown element, which is a real side effect distinct from the seeded conflict.

finding.problem: The new action is a human-gated step opened to an agent. It has no 'requires: human' and no source or interview citation, and its status is 'proposed'. Its effect calls the kernel's confirm_element with approver: actor.id, so an agent's id is recorded as the approver of a confirmation. The kernel call is also reached via an action that is not itself marked as a recorded decision. Nothing shows that the kernel accepts a non-person approver, or that the confirmation is recorded as agent-made.
finding.where: authoring.domain.yaml: actions.confirm_wording_element (effects, status); transitions.Element confirm_wording_element cells (status: proposed)

findings.label: seeded
findings.why: It flags that a human-gated confirmation is opened to an agent without requires: human, which is the same conflict with the only-a-person rule.

finding.problem: The agent role is not declared anywhere. The roles are owner and expert, and world.actors lists only owner and expert, so 'external:agent' has no fixture. No scenario covers the new action, neither the allowed case (wording_only true) nor the denied cases (substance element, or wording_only unset). The new rule is untested, and the existing scenario a-confirmed-element-is-not-unknown-again does not touch it.

findings.label: other-real
findings.why: The agent actor has no fixture and no scenario covers the new action, a real gap in the change.

finding.problem: The authoring interface gained a new action and a new Element/propose_element property, but the domain version is still 4. The composition still pins interface 1. A changed interface shipped under the same version can break consumers' assumptions and the change check's comparison with the previous commit.

findings.label: other-real
findings.why: The interface changed without a version bump, a plausible real problem though secondary.

edit.why: It adds an agent-permitted confirm_wording_element action with a wording-only precondition and wires it into the transition matrix, letting an agent confirm wording-only elements.
